name: Gilgamesh: A Verse Narrative
date: Copyright 1970 (Houghton Mifflin, Boston); hardcover commonly dated 1971; Mentor/New American Library paperback April 1972 with an afterword by John H. Marks; Mariner/Houghton Mifflin reissue 2003. Finalist, 1972 National Book Award for Translation.
creator: Herbert Mason (born 1932), poet and later University Professor of History and Religious Thought at Boston University, best known otherwise as translator of Louis Massignon's The Passion of al-Hallaj. Afterword (1972 paperback) by John H. Marks, Princeton Old Testament scholar.
form: Free-verse narrative in four numbered parts (I to IV), with unrhymed lines of irregular length grouped in verse paragraphs and '***' section breaks. Back matter: a glossary ('Names and Places Appearing in the Narrative'), an essay 'About the Gilgamesh', an 'Autobiographical Postscript', and the Marks afterword. A retelling, not a line-by-line translation.
translator_access: Mason did not work from the cuneiform. His postscript calls the book 'a subjective evocation' 'based on literal scholarly translations', and the Marks afterword states that 'the author makes no claim to present an accurate rendering of the cuneiform text.' His entry point was E. A. Speiser's English translation, read in 1954 in Albert Lord's Harvard course on oral epic. He later took a Harvard doctorate in Near Eastern Languages and Literatures (his field was Arabic and Islamic mysticism), but the book itself is built from existing English, German and French versions.
scholarly_adviser: No single named crib-supplier. Sources are the published translations of Heidel, Speiser, Campbell Thompson, Ebeling and Contenau. Personal influences named in the postscript: Albert Lord (Harvard), Louis Massignon (Collège de France), Père Henri Cazelles (Institut Catholique, Paris), Madeleine David. John H. Marks supplied the scholarly afterword for the 1972 edition.
versions_used: The Standard Babylonian (Nineveh) epic as mediated by pre-1960 translations: Alexander Heidel, The Gilgamesh Epic and Old Testament Parallels (2nd ed., 1949); E. A. Speiser in Pritchard's Ancient Near Eastern Texts (2nd ed., 1955); R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish (1928/1930); Erich Ebeling in Gressmann's Altorientalische Texte zum Alten Testament (1926); G. Contenau, L'Epopée de Gilgamesh (1939). Old Babylonian material entered only as those translators had already merged it (e.g. Siduri's advice 'The gods gave death to man and kept life for themselves' is the OB Sippar tablet speech). No Sumerian poems used directly; no post-1970 finds (Sulaymaniyah tablet etc.) since it predates them.
non_standard_material: Silent merge. Nothing in the poem signals which tablet or version a passage comes from, and Mason freely reorders and invents: Enlil is 'merged in the present narrative with Ninurta, the war god'; Urshanabi's role 'is greatly reduced'; Utnapishtim is made monotheistic ('The monotheism of Utnapishtim in this narration will have to be accepted by these scholars as part of any modern retelling'). He also puts invented speeches in characters' mouths, e.g. Enkidu's long deathbed meditation on the gods' drunken contest to create wretchedness, and Utnapishtim's lines 'love is wrung from our inmost heart', which echo a 1959 letter from Massignon quoted in the postscript. Only the Tablet XII material is flagged, and that is quarantined in the back-matter essay.
gap_policy: Smoothed over completely. Lacunae are bridged with Mason's own narrative so the story reads as continuous; the reader is never told that the source is broken. [uncertain: no passage-by-passage check against Speiser was possible]
typography_of_absence: Nothing that marks textual loss. No brackets, no editorial ellipses, no blank space for missing lines. The only visual breaks are '***' scene dividers and part numerals. The single ellipsis found ('dead and . . .' in Enkidu's dying speech) is dramatic, marking his voice failing, not a lacuna.
tablet_xii: Dropped from the narrative. The essay 'About the Gilgamesh' summarises Tablet XII (Enkidu's descent to retrieve lost objects, his illusory return) and the Sumerian Death of Gilgamesh, then says: 'These and other stories about Gilgamesh have not been included in the present narrative for reasons of dramatic unity.' Mason then appends a short verse 'afterglimpse' based on the Tablet XII reunion, labelled 'an interpretation only', in which Enkidu's shade tells Gilgamesh 'You must not touch me' and Gilgamesh ends by walking out toward the sound of celebration. The main poem therefore ends at the walls, and Tablet XII is recast as a grief coda rather than an underworld report.
turning_point: Enkidu's death is the hinge, and the whole book is built around it. The opening lines announce the subject as grief rather than kingship: 'It is an old story / But one that can still be told / About a man who loved / And lost a friend to death / And learned he lacked the power / To bring him back to life.' Everything before Part III is set-up for the loss. Part III opens with 'Gilgamesh wept bitterly for his friend' and follows with Mason's longest authorial meditation, a passage on bereavement that leaves the story altogether ('All that is left to one who grieves / Is convalescence. No change of heart or spiritual / Conversion, for the heart has changed'). The quest is recast as grief-work: Gilgamesh seeks eternal life 'Which he might carry back to give his friend', a motive the ancient text does not state. The snake is a second, smaller hinge that ends the journey ('In time he recognized this loss / As the end of his journey'), but it registers as a repetition of the first loss, not a new one.
arc_interpretation: Grief and acceptance, framed autobiographically. Mason's postscript ties the book to his father's death when he was seven and to the death of his Harvard friend Jack Kotteman from Hodgkin's disease in the mid-1950s; he calls the book 'for those who have known loss' and describes Gilgamesh as a story 'understood immediately by anyone who has suffered loss, a loss one has yearned to restore and finally has had to accept.' He follows Albert Lord in reading Gilgamesh as a kind of antihero whose only heroism is to keep walking. Kingship almost vanishes: after Enkidu dies 'He was no more a king / But just a man who now had lost his way.' Maturity through city-building is muted; the SB frame of the proud king showing off his walls is replaced by a man whose townspeople have forgotten his friend's name. The back-matter essay leaves the verdict open ('the reader must decide what that ending means for himself'), offering either tragic despair or the hope 'that for the human being the experience of wisdom is more important than possession of even the highest things.' The Marks afterword endorses this reading: the book is 'an attempt to convey the profound anguish Gilgamesh suffered after his constant companion and friend, Enkidu, died.'
key_passages: Shamhat and Enkidu: the woman is unnamed ('the woman', later 'her'), and the scene is explicit but brief and tender: 'She took his hand and guided it / Across her breasts and between her legs / And touched him with her fingers / Gently and bent down and moistened / Him with her lips then drew him / Slowly to the ground.' Enkidu afterwards feels 'a strange exhaustion, / As if life had left his body' as the animals leave him. On his deathbed he blames her: 'She made me see / Things as a man, and a man sees death in things. / That is what it is to be a man.' Siduri's advice: kept, compressed and made maternal ('She spoke as to a child who could not understand'): 'The gods gave death to man and kept life for / Themselves. That is the only way it is. / Cherish your rests; the children you might have; / You are a thing that carries so much tiredness.' She washes and dresses him and he throws the clothes off, returning to 'the dark pelts'. Death in the bedchamber (Tablet XI): the SB line 'in my bedchamber death dwells' is not rendered as such; the nearest equivalent comes after the sleep test with the seven loaves: 'Wherever I go (even here) I am drawn back / To death.' [original uses dashes] Utnapishtim is recast as a wise, half-blind mystic who speaks of friendship ('Friendship is vowing toward immortality / And does not know the passing away of beauty'). The snake: 'A serpent had smelled its sweet fragrance and saw / Its chance to come from the water, and devoured / The plant, shedding its skin as slough... He sat / Down on the ground, and wept.' Walls of Uruk: no Urshanabi tour and no repetition of the prologue's praise of brickwork. Instead Gilgamesh asks a blind old man if he has heard the name Enkidu, is met with a shrug, and then 'He looked at the walls, / Awed at the heights / His people had achieved / And for a moment (just a moment) / All that lay behind him / Passed from view.'
diction_and_metre: Loose free verse, mostly short to medium unrhymed lines with conversational, modern American idiom and occasional bluntness ('a man who had no balls'). No archaism, no attempt at Akkadian parallelism or repetition formulas, few epithets. Long stretches of authorial commentary and psychological narration sit alongside the plot, and Mason admits 'At times my line of narration is very prosy indeed.' Speech is often unpunctuated by quotation marks and folded into the verse. Danny Yee's comparative review groups it with the 'freer versions', noting it rearranges tablet material and uses paragraph white-space.
sample_line: "It is an old story / But one that can still be told / About a man who loved / And lost a friend to death / And learned he lacked the power / To bring him back to life." (Mason, Gilgamesh: A Verse Narrative, opening of Part I)
critical_response: Finalist for the 1972 National Book Award in Translation (National Book Foundation). Publisher copy calls it 'the most widely read and enduring interpretation' of the epic and 'a triumph of scholarship, a masterpiece of style, and a labor of love'. John H. Marks's afterword calls it 'a sensitive, authentic retelling' with 'its own spellbinding power, evoking feelings and thoughts familiar to all who suffer the loss of loved companions', while conceding it is not an accurate rendering of the cuneiform. Danny Yee's comparative review (dannyreviews.com) treats it as 'a subjective evocation' and one of the freer versions, choice between it and Ferry being 'a matter of taste'. It became a long-running classroom text in US college survey courses. [uncertain: no contemporary 1971-72 newspaper reviews located]
controversies: The main dispute is category: a book its own author calls a 'subjective evocation', not a translation, was shortlisted for a national award in Translation. Mason anticipated scholarly objection to his 'cavalier view of the gods' and to Utnapishtim's monotheism. Its liberties (invented speeches, reordered episodes, reduced Urshanabi, merged gods, excluded Tablet XII) make it unreliable as a guide to the ancient text, a point Marks's afterword concedes. No provenance or authorship dispute.
regional_reception: No evidence found of Arabic, Kurdish or Iraqi translation or reception; its reach appears to be English-language and mainly American academic. [uncertain]
ai_craft_tension: Mason is the purest case of the poet who adds nothing a machine could extract from the tablets and everything a machine could not. He worked entirely from other people's literal translations, so on the philological side he contributed zero; his value is the fifteen years of 'inward companionship and meditation' he describes, plus a specific bereavement. The book's most memorable parts are ones no source contains: Enkidu's rant about drunk gods competing to make misery, the meditation on grief as 'convalescence', the blind man who has never heard of Enkidu. A model can reproduce Speiser, and can paraphrase Speiser freely, but the reason readers still pick up Mason is that the reframing comes from a person who had lost someone and says so in a postscript. It also shows the cost: his version erases the gaps, the multiple layers of the text and the gods' theology, so it is a reading, not a record. For an essay on AI and craft, Mason stands for the claim that interpretation is authored by lived experience, and for the risk that a fluent, gap-free retelling can pass for the thing itself (here, to the point of a Translation award shortlist).
essay_hooks: 1) Shortlisted for the 1972 National Book Award in Translation although the author says he could not render the cuneiform and calls it 'a subjective evocation' (NBF page; Mason's postscript). 2) Origin story: a Harvard junior in 1954 skips Albert Lord's lectures to hide in an empty room in Emerson Hall writing his own Gilgamesh in longhand; the same year a friend, Jack Kotteman, is diagnosed with Hodgkin's disease and dies within two years (Autobiographical Postscript). 3) Fifteen years in the making: 'All told it has been fifteen years since I began working on "my Gilgamesh"' (postscript). 4) Massignon's instruction: 'You must decide the end. You must finish your Gilgamesh.' (postscript). 5) The ending swap: instead of the king proudly showing off his walls, Gilgamesh asks a blind man if he knows the name Enkidu and gets a shrug (Part IV). 6) Mason's Utnapishtim speaks his mentor's letter: 'love is wrung from our inmost heart', echoing Massignon's 1959 'Love was to surrender, to be wrung from our inmost heart'. 7) 'This narrative is, in one important sense, for those who have known loss.'
